\chapter{Six Verbs at the Core}
\label{ch:pa-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name six everyday Punjabi verbs by the -\pa{ਣਾ}/-\pa{ਨਾ} ending, strip that ending to reach the stem, trace each one to its Sanskrit and Indo-European root, and explain how the lost breathy consonants left Punjabi with a tone no other major Indo-Aryan language has.}

The sixth verb runs the whole chapter at once: hold the doubled n that keeps jāṇnā apart from jāṇā, separate the two \pa{ਜ} that came from different Sanskrit sounds, strip the stem off all six infinitives, and state that none of them carries a tone.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hoṇā]{\pa{ਹੋਣਾ} — “to be,” and the two old verbs braided inside it}

\label{lesson:PA-C07-hona}



\begin{quote}
You have been saying \textbf{\pa{ਹੈ}} \emph{hai}, “is,” since Chapter 2. Here is the verb it belongs to — and it sounds nothing like it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਹੋਣਾ}} — \emph{hoṇā} — \textbf{to be}
\end{quote}

Four shapes, hanging from the top line: \textbf{\pa{ਹ}} \emph{h}, with the \textbf{\pa{ੋ}} sign on it for \emph{o}; then \textbf{\pa{ਣ}}, an \emph{n} made with the tongue tip curled back; then \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} for long \emph{ā}. It reads \emph{ho-ṇā}.

The ending \textbf{-\pa{ਣਾ}} \emph{-ṇā} is how Punjabi names a verb — the same ending that sat on \emph{bolṇā}. English names a verb by putting a word in front of it, \emph{to be}; Punjabi puts an ending on the back and never uses a separate word. Take that ending off and what remains is the \textbf{stem}: \textbf{ho-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hoṇā} comes from Sanskrit \emph{bhavati}, “becomes,” built on the root \emph{bhū-}. Middle Indo-Aryan softened that \emph{bh-} to \emph{h-}, so \emph{bhavati} thinned to \emph{hoi} and then to \textbf{hoṇā}.

The root is Indo-European, *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}uH-}, “grow, become.” English keeps it in \textbf{be} and \textbf{been}, and — by way of “the place where one dwells” — in \textbf{build}, \textbf{booth}, and \textbf{bower}. Latin held it as \emph{fuī} “I was” and \emph{futūrus}, which English borrowed as \textbf{future}. Greek held it as \emph{phúsis} “nature,” which English borrowed as \textbf{physics}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one verb, two roots}]
Chapter 2 traced \textbf{\pa{ਹੈ}} \emph{hai} to a different Sanskrit verb altogether — \emph{asti}, “is,” the root behind English \textbf{is}, Latin \emph{est}, German \emph{ist}. So Punjabi's “to be” is \textbf{two ancient verbs braided into one}: the name and the stem come from \emph{bhū-}, the everyday present tense comes from \emph{as-}.

English braids the very same two, at the very same seam, and nobody notices: \emph{am, is, are} belong to the \emph{as-} verb; \emph{be, being, been} belong to the \emph{b\textsuperscript{h}uH-} verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hoṇā} — to be
  \item \emph{Strip:} \textbf{hoṇā} minus \textbf{-ṇā} leaves the stem \textbf{ho-}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{hoṇā} $\leftarrow$ \emph{bhavati} $\to$ English \textbf{be}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{hai} $\leftarrow$ \emph{asti} $\to$ English \textbf{is}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending names a Punjabi verb, and what is left of \emph{hoṇā} once you take it off? (\textbf{-ṇā}; the stem \textbf{ho-}.) And why do \emph{hoṇā} and \emph{hai} not resemble each other at all? (They are two different ancient verbs braided into one — the \emph{bhū-} verb and the \emph{as-} verb, exactly as English braids \emph{be} with \emph{is}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jāṇā]{\pa{ਜਾਣਾ} — “to go,” and a sound law you can run yourself}

\label{lesson:PA-C07-jana}



\begin{quote}
Name the ending that turns a Punjabi stem into the verb's plain name. (\textbf{-\pa{ਣਾ}} \emph{-ṇā}.) Here is the second verb to wear it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਜਾਣਾ}} — \emph{jāṇā} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\pa{ਜ}} \emph{j}, then \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} long \emph{ā}, then \textbf{\pa{ਣ}} — the curled-back \emph{ṇ} you already met inside \emph{hoṇā} — then \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} again. Nothing new to decode. Strip the \textbf{-\pa{ਣਾ}} and the stem is \textbf{jā-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jāṇā} is Sanskrit \emph{yāti}, “goes,” on the root \emph{yā-}, “travel.” The \emph{y} became a \emph{j}, and that was not an accident about this one word. Early Indo-Aryan turned \textbf{every} initial \emph{y-} into \emph{j-} on the way to Punjabi, and the change is regular enough to run backwards yourself:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Sanskrit \emph{yoga} $\to$ Punjabi \textbf{jog}
  \item Sanskrit \emph{yuvan} “young” $\to$ Punjabi \textbf{javān}
  \item Sanskrit \emph{yamunā}, the river $\to$ Punjabi \textbf{Jamnā}
\end{itemize}

So a Sanskrit word beginning \emph{y-} is very often a Punjabi word you half know already, hiding behind a \emph{j}.

The root itself is Indo-European, *\emph{yeh\textsubscript{2}-}, “to go, travel” — the same verb as Lithuanian \emph{jóti}, “to ride.” It is one of the rare cases where English inherited nothing usable, so the prize here is the rule, not the cousin.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jāṇā} — to go
  \item \emph{Strip:} \textbf{jāṇā} minus \textbf{-ṇā} leaves the stem \textbf{jā-}
  \item \emph{Run the rule:} \emph{yoga} $\to$ \textbf{jog}, \emph{yuvan} $\to$ \textbf{javān}, \emph{yamunā} $\to$ \textbf{Jamnā}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{jāṇā} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{yāti}, “goes”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Sanskrit verb is \emph{jāṇā}, and what happened to its first sound? (\emph{Yāti}, “goes”; the \emph{y-} became \emph{j-}.) Give one more word the same change caught. (\emph{Jog}, \emph{javān}, or \emph{Jamnā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āuṇā]{\pa{ਆਉਣਾ} — “to come,” which is “go” pointed back at you}

\label{lesson:PA-C07-auna}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{jāṇā}, “to go.” Its opposite is not a different verb. It is the same verb with one small piece stuck on the front.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਆਉਣਾ}} — \emph{āuṇā} — \textbf{to come}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\pa{ਆ}} is a whole syllable on its own, long \emph{ā}: a Punjabi word cannot start with a bare vowel sign, so a vowel that opens a word rides a carrier letter. Then \textbf{\pa{ਉ}} for \emph{u}, then the familiar \textbf{\pa{ਣਾ}} ending. It reads \emph{ā-u-ṇā}, three beats. The stem is \textbf{ā-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{āuṇā} goes back to Sanskrit \emph{ā-gacchati}, “comes.” Take that apart and it is the prefix \textbf{ā-}, “toward, hither,” sitting on the verb \textbf{gam-}, “go.” Punjabi's “come” is literally \emph{go-toward-me}, and the \emph{g} wore away over the centuries until only the rounded \emph{-u-} was left of it.

That prefix is a tool, not a one-off: Punjabi keeps \emph{ā-} in the sense of motion \textbf{toward} the speaker, the same job English does with a separate word.

And \textbf{gam-} is the good part. It is Indo-European *\emph{g\textsuperscript{w}em-}, “to step, go” — and English inherited it straight down the Germanic line as \textbf{come}. Latin took the same root as \emph{venīre}, which English then borrowed back many times over: \textbf{advent}, \textbf{invent}, \textbf{convene}, \textbf{venue}, \textbf{event}, \textbf{revenue}, \textbf{intervene}, \textbf{souvenir}. Greek took it as \emph{baínein}, “to step,” giving English \textbf{base}, \textbf{basis}, and \textbf{acrobat}.

So when a Punjabi speaker says \emph{ā}, the second syllable of that word is the same ancient step as your own \emph{come}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jāṇā} to go, then \textbf{āuṇā} to come
  \item \emph{Split:} \textbf{ā-} toward, plus \textbf{gam-} go
  \item \emph{Connect:} \emph{gam-} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{g\textsuperscript{w}em-} $\to$ English \textbf{come}, \textbf{advent}, \textbf{acrobat}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces are inside \emph{āuṇā}? (The prefix \emph{ā-}, “toward,” and the old verb \emph{gam-}, “go.”) Which everyday English verb is that second piece? (\textbf{Come}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khāṇā]{\pa{ਖਾਣਾ} — “to eat,” and the tone hiding one letter away}

\label{lesson:PA-C07-khana}



\begin{quote}
This verb is easy. Its neighbour in the alphabet is the strangest thing in the whole language, and this is where you meet it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਖਾਣਾ}} — \emph{khāṇā} — \textbf{to eat}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\pa{ਖ}} is \emph{kh}: a \emph{k} with a puff of breath after it, as in English \emph{back-hand} said fast. Then \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}, then the ending \textbf{\pa{ਣਾ}}. The stem is \textbf{khā-}.

It comes straight from Sanskrit \emph{khādati}, “chews, eats.” No English cousin has been securely traced from that root, and that is fine — the prize in this word is its \textbf{sound}.

\begin{sounds}
Gurmukhi keeps its consonants in rows of five. The \emph{k}-row runs \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} \emph{ka}, \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} \emph{kha}, \textbf{\pa{ਗ}} \emph{ga}, \textbf{\pa{ਘ}} — and that fourth letter was once \emph{gha}, a \emph{g} said with a breathy voice.

Punjabi lost those breathy-voiced sounds. It did \textbf{not} lose the words. When \textbf{\pa{ਘ}} \emph{gh} starts a word it is now said as a plain \emph{k}, and everything the old consonant carried moved onto the vowel as a \textbf{low, rising pitch}. Same elsewhere in the word, in mirror image: the pitch falls instead.

That leaves pairs which are spelled differently and pronounced identically, apart from the tune:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Punjabi} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\pa{ਘੋੜਾ}} horse & \emph{kòṛā}, pitch dipping then rising \\
\textbf{\pa{ਕੋੜਾ}} whip & \emph{koṛā}, pitch level \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two words, one string of consonants and vowels, and the only difference is music. That makes Punjabi the one major Indo-Aryan language with \textbf{tone} — Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Gujarati, and Marathi have nothing like it.

Your \textbf{\pa{ਖਾਣਾ}} is safe: \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} \emph{kh} is voiceless, it never had the breathy voice, so it never traded anything for a tone. \emph{Khāṇā} is said flat.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{khāṇā} — to eat — flat, no tune
  \item the pair — \emph{kòṛā} horse, dipping; then \emph{koṛā} whip, level
  \item the rule — the old breathy \emph{gh} went and left a pitch behind
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates \emph{kòṛā} “horse” from \emph{koṛā} “whip”? (Pitch alone — the first dips and rises.) Where did that pitch come from? (From \textbf{\pa{ਘ}}, an old breathy \emph{gh} that stopped being breathy.) And does \emph{khāṇā} carry one? (No — \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} \emph{kh} has no voice to lose.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vekhṇā]{\pa{ਵੇਖਣਾ} — “to see,” a verb built out of the eye itself}

\label{lesson:PA-C07-vekhna}



\begin{quote}
The \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} \emph{kh} you learned in \emph{khāṇā} turns up again here, in the middle of a word this time. Same puff of breath, same flat pitch.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਵੇਖਣਾ}} — \emph{vekhṇā} — \textbf{to see, to look}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\pa{ਵ}} \emph{v}, with the \textbf{\pa{ੇ}} sign on it for \emph{e}; then \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} \emph{kh}; then the ending \textbf{\pa{ਣਾ}}. It reads \emph{vekh-ṇā}, and the stem is \textbf{vekh-}.

Punjabi also says \textbf{\pa{ਦੇਖਣਾ}} \emph{dekhṇā} for the same thing, which is the form Hindi settled on. One word, two front consonants, both alive in Punjabi — \emph{vekhṇā} is the more homely, more Punjabi-sounding of the two.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vekhṇā} comes from Sanskrit \emph{prekṣate}, “looks at” — the prefix \emph{pra-}, “forth,” on the verb \emph{īkṣ-}, “see.” And \emph{īkṣ-} is built on \emph{akṣi}, the Sanskrit word for the \textbf{eye}. Punjabi's verb for seeing is, underneath, the organ you do it with.

That noun is Indo-European, *\emph{h\textsubscript{3}ek\textsuperscript{w}-}, and English is full of it. Inherited plainly: \textbf{eye} — and \textbf{window}, borrowed from Norse \emph{vindauga}, a “wind-eye,” the hole that let the smoke out. Borrowed from Latin \emph{oculus}: \textbf{ocular}, \textbf{binoculars}, \textbf{inoculate}. Borrowed from Greek \emph{ōps} and \emph{optikós}: \textbf{optic}, \textbf{optician}, \textbf{autopsy} (seeing for oneself), \textbf{synopsis}, \textbf{myopia}.

So \emph{vekhṇā}, \emph{eye}, \emph{window}, and \emph{autopsy} are four settlements of one very old word for the thing in your head.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{vekhṇā} — to see — then its twin \textbf{dekhṇā}
  \item \emph{Strip:} \textbf{vekhṇā} minus \textbf{-ṇā} leaves \textbf{vekh-}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \emph{īkṣ-} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{h\textsubscript{3}ek\textsuperscript{w}-} $\to$ English \textbf{eye}, \textbf{optic}, \textbf{window}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What noun is hiding inside \emph{vekhṇā}? (The \textbf{eye} — Sanskrit \emph{akṣi}, behind the verb \emph{īkṣ-}.) Name two English words off that root. (Any of \textbf{eye}, \textbf{window}, \textbf{ocular}, \textbf{optic}, \textbf{autopsy}.) And what is the Hindi-shaped twin of this verb? (\emph{Dekhṇā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Every wellbeing atom returns at R3}

\label{lesson:PA-R07-wellbeing-r3}



\begin{quote}
No new language. Listen once, then speak two short turns. Keep each score independent and repair only a miss.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
1. Listen to \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?} and give its meaning before repeating it. 2. Reply \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ} from the English cue alone. 3. Answer thanks with \emph{koī gall nahīṁ}. 4. Name the three small root cues: question \emph{k-}, first-person \emph{m-}, negative \emph{n-}.

Romanization is only a machine-readable record of prior speech. It is not Gurmukhi reading or writing evidence.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask, answer, and close the exchange once more from meaning alone.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jāṇnā]{\pa{ਜਾਣਨਾ} — “to know,” one letter from “to go”}

\label{lesson:PA-C07-janna}



\begin{quote}
Run the five you have — \emph{hoṇā, jāṇā, āuṇā, khāṇā, vekhṇā} — and pull the stem off each one. The sixth is the closest of them all to English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਜਾਣਨਾ}} — \emph{jāṇnā} — \textbf{to know}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\pa{ਜ}} \emph{j}, \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} long \emph{ā}, then \textbf{\pa{ਣ}} — the curled-back \emph{ṇ} — and then a second, different \emph{n}: \textbf{\pa{ਨ}}, made with the tongue on the teeth. Then \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}. Both are pronounced, one after the other: \emph{jāṇ-nā}, held long across the seam, the way English does in \emph{thin-ness}.

That second letter is the whole difference between \textbf{\pa{ਜਾਣਾ}} \emph{jāṇā} “to go” and \textbf{\pa{ਜਾਣਨਾ}} \emph{jāṇnā} “to know.” The stem here is \textbf{jāṇ-}, and because it already ends in the curled-back \emph{ṇ}, the infinitive shows up in its other shape, plain \textbf{-\pa{ਨਾ}} \emph{-nā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jāṇnā} continues Sanskrit \emph{jānāti}, on the root \emph{jñā-}, “know.” Note what that means for the rule from \emph{jāṇā}: these two Punjabi verbs both open with \textbf{\pa{ਜ}} \emph{j}, but from different sources — \emph{jāṇā}'s \emph{j} was a Sanskrit \emph{y}, while \emph{jāṇnā}'s was already there, in \emph{jñā-}.

That root is Indo-European *\emph{ǵneh\textsubscript{3}-}, and English is stuffed with it. Down the Germanic line: \textbf{know}, \textbf{knowledge}, \textbf{can} (once “to know how”), \textbf{cunning}, \textbf{ken}, and \textbf{uncouth}, which is “un-known.” Borrowed from Latin \emph{(g)nōscere}: \textbf{notice}, \textbf{note}, \textbf{notion}, \textbf{cognition}, \textbf{recognize}, \textbf{acquaint}, \textbf{narrate}, and \textbf{ignore} — “not to know.” Borrowed from Greek \emph{gnōsis}: \textbf{diagnosis}, \textbf{prognosis}, \textbf{agnostic}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{jāṇā} to go, then \textbf{jāṇnā} to know, holding the long \emph{n}
  \item \emph{Run all six:} \emph{hoṇā, jāṇā, āuṇā, khāṇā, vekhṇā, jāṇnā}, stripping each stem
  \item \emph{Say it:} the two sources — \emph{jāṇā}'s \emph{j} from \emph{yā-}, \emph{jāṇnā}'s from \emph{jñā-}
  \item \emph{Say it:} not one of the six carries a tone — every stem is flat
  \item \emph{Connect:} \emph{jñā-} $\to$ English \textbf{know}, \textbf{notice}, \textbf{diagnosis}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What single written mark separates \emph{jāṇā} from \emph{jāṇnā}? (A second \emph{n}, the dental \textbf{\pa{ਨ}}, held long in speech.) Where did each verb's \emph{j} come from? (\emph{Jāṇā}'s from a Sanskrit \emph{y-}; \emph{jāṇnā}'s from \emph{jñā-}.) And which English verb is the very same word as \emph{jāṇnā}? (\textbf{Know}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
